evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.47: ex plānīs autem circulus aut orbis
terms.comment: The plain Latin word for the figure, which Cicero gives as the Latin for Greek κύκλος, beside orbis. It also means a ring, a hoop, and a circle of people (see “hoop” and “group”). To draw one is circulum dūcere, as līneam dūcere is to draw a line; Ovid says orbem dūcere of the compasses.

terms.gloss: a circle, a ring, anything round and flat
evidence: Quint. 1.10.41: sī efficiet orbem, quae fōrma est in plānīs maximē perfecta
Ov. Met. 8.249: pars altera dūceret orbem
terms.comment: The round shape in general, a disc or a ring as much as the line; in orbem is “in a circle” (Caes. B.G. 5.33: in orbem cōnsisterent, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Dūc circulum crētā, deinde in mediō duōs oculōs et ōs: ecce faciēs!
phrases.english: Draw a circle with the chalk, then two eyes and a mouth in the middle: there’s a face!

phrases.latin: Rotae circulī sunt; quadrātae nōn volverentur.
phrases.english: Wheels are circles; square ones wouldn’t roll.

phrases.latin: cumque duae fōrmae praestantissimae sint, ex solidīs globus … ex plānīs autem circulus aut orbis
phrases.english: and since there are two most excellent shapes, among the solids the sphere, among the plane figures the circle, or round

phrases.latin: prīmus et ex ūnō duo ferrea bracchia nōdō vīnxit, ut aequālī spatiō distantibus illīs altera pars stāret, pars altera dūceret orbem
phrases.english: he was the first to join two iron arms at one knot, so that, with the two held the same distance apart, one leg stood still and the other drew a circle
